# Experimental Demonstration of an Acoustic Asymmetric Diffraction Grating Based on Passive Parity-Time-Symmetric Medium

Yuzhen Yang $^{ID}$ , $^{1,2}$ Han Jia $^{ID}$ , $^{1,2,3,*}$ Yafeng Bi, $^{1,2}$ Han Zhao, $^{1,2}$ and Jun Yang $^{1,2,3,\dagger}$

$^{1}$ Key Laboratory of Noise and Vibration Research, Institute of Acoustics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, People's Republic of China

$^{2}$ University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, People's Republic of China $^{3}$ State Key Laboratory of Acoustics, Institute of Acoustics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, People's Republic of China

(Received 24 April 2019; revised manuscript received 16 August 2019; published 19 September 2019)

A passive parity-time (PT) symmetric medium provides a feasible scheme to experimentally investigate non-Hermitian systems. We experimentally demonstrate an acoustic asymmetric diffraction grating based on a designed passive PT-symmetric medium. The proposed passive PT-symmetric medium is composed of additional cavities and leaked holes. By skillfully combining these two unit cells, the composite unit cell can simultaneously modulate the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index. When the modulation amplitudes of the real and imaginary parts are equal, asymmetric diffraction is observed in both simulated and experimental results at an exceptional point. Compared to the previous design method of a passive PT-symmetric medium, the proposed scheme could prevent the influence of interferential diffraction beams and enhance the diffraction ability with more compact modulation. In addition, the designed metamaterial structure provides a practical way to construct passive PT-symmetric acoustic potential and opens alternative possibilities for further investigation of acoustic wave control in non-Hermitian systems.

DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevApplied.12.034040

## I. INTRODUCTION

Parity-time (PT) symmetry is a concept arising from quantum mechanics, which means the invariance of Hamiltonian under parity-time inversion. The Hermitian property existing in the Hamiltonian was considered to be a guarantee of real spectra corresponding to observable physical quantities until 1998, when Bender and Boettcher confirmed that the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian could still possess real spectra in a complex system with PT-symmetry [1]. For maintenance of PT-symmetry, a necessary but not sufficient condition is that the complex potential should obey a function of position as $V(\mathbf{r}) = V^{*}(-\mathbf{r})$ , where \* is a conjugate symbol. A most important characteristic of a PT-symmetric system is the spontaneous breaking from the unbroken phase to a broken phase at a threshold of the complex potential [2–5]. In recent years, non-Hermitian systems with PT-symmetric potential have been widely discussed in fields of classic waves because of the similarity between the Schrödinger equation and the classic wave equation [5–30]. Many unconventional phenomena of PT-symmetry have been successively demonstrated in optics, including Bloch oscillation [6,7], optical isolation [8,9], unidirectional invisibility or reflectionless effect [10–12], and coherent perfect absorption and lasing [15–20,31]. In addition, many interesting acoustic effects, such as one-way cloak [32], invisible sensing [22], and sound absorption [33], have also been extensively studied.

PT-symmetric media need both real and imaginary modulations, which increases the difficulty of designing available structures. In acoustics, C. Shi and R. Fleury achieved gain using loudspeakers to inject sound energy into the system $[5,22]$ . However, it is cumbersome and complex to realize periodical gain using loudspeakers. To overcome the difficulties of fabricating the gain part, researchers introduced passive PT-symmetric media with similar properties to study the characteristics of PT-symmetric systems $[11,19,34–36]$ . Previous works mainly paid attention to PT-symmetry in one-dimensional waveguides in which waves propagate along with the direction of modulation. To enhance the practicability and applicability of PT-symmetric systems, higher dimensional systems have been subsequently studied in recent years $[35–37]$ . Diffraction grating as a basic device in multidimensional space has attracted much attention recently $[36–40]$ . Conventional diffraction gratings with only real modulation of the refractive index offer a pair of equal and opposite wave vectors. However, periodical PT-symmetric gratings could offer a unidirectional wave vector at an exceptional point (EP) with $n_{r}=n_{i}$ . Previously, optical asymmetric diffraction based on a PT-symmetric medium has been theoretically discussed [36,37]. Research of acoustic PT-symmetric gratings is also meaningful for manipulation of acoustic propagation. However, the passive PT-symmetric unit cell used in the unidirectional acoustic focus [35] is not suitable to design the diffraction grating for its anisotropic property.

In this paper, we design an acoustic asymmetric diffraction grating (AADG) in two-dimensional space utilizing all passive unit cells composed of additional cavities and leaked holes. It is convenient to obtain a balanced complex potential by modulating the heights of additional cavities and the radii of the leaked holes. In both simulated and experimental results, the positive first-order diffraction with a negative incident Bragg angle is suppressed at EP while the negative first-order diffraction with a positive incident angle is not affected. This seems to be the first experiment to demonstrate the asymmetric diffraction of a PT-symmetric grating. This AADG has potential applications in many fields, such as beam forming, ultrasonic medical imaging, and directional noise reduction.

## II. EXPERIMENT AND RESULTS

## A. Basic model of a PT-symmetric acoustic grating

In acoustics, a PT-symmetric medium can be realized with a complex refractive index obeying the condition of $n(\mathbf{r}) = n^{*}(-\mathbf{r})$ . As shown in the top panel of Fig. 1(a), the classic PT-symmetric medium has simple harmonic modulation of the refractive index $n'(x) = n_{r} \cos(hx) + in_{i} \sin(hx)$ , where $n'$ denotes the modulated part of the refractive index and $n_{r}, n_{i}$ denote the real and imaginary amplitudes of modulation, respectively. To simplify the structural design requirement, previous researchers adopted a complex square-wave modulation instead of the simple harmonic modulation. In addition, the manual truncation of the refractive index and in-phase shift of the real part spatially separates the modulations of the real and imaginary parts [middle panel of Fig. 1(a)]. It has been proven that the features of EP in an exact PT-symmetric system can still be observed and controlled in a passive PT-symmetric system [11,19,34–36]. However, this adjustment artificially doubles the modulation period, which will introduce unwanted first-order disturbance and reduce the diffraction ability in a grating. To avoid these above deficiencies of existing passive PT-symmetric media, we change the period back to that of an exact PT-symmetric medium. As shown in the bottom panel of Fig. 1(a), a complex square-wave modulation is still adopted but with spatial overlap of the real and imaginary parts. The densities of real and imaginary modulations are doubled compared to existing PT-symmetric media, which will enhance the diffraction ability of the AADG.

The schematic model of the AADG based on the revised PT-symmetric medium is shown in Fig. 1(b). $n_{1}^{\prime}$ , $n_{2}^{\prime}$ , and $n_{3}^{\prime}$ represent the real modulated part, imaginary modulated part, and overlap of real and imaginary modulated parts, respectively. At Bragg incident angles, there are two main coupled diffracted waves propagating in the AADG. A general expression of sound pressure in the grating is written as $P(\mathbf{r}) = A_{0}e^{-i\mathbf{q}_{0}\mathbf{r}} + A_{h}e^{-i\mathbf{q}_{h}\mathbf{r}}$ , where $A_{0}, A_{h}$ are amplitudes of the zero-order diffraction and the positive first-order (negative first-order) diffraction, respectively. The diffractive coefficients can be calculated using coupled-mode theory (see Appendix). When the sign of the Bragg incident angle is negative, that is, $-\theta_{B}$ , the relationship for the amplitudes of diffracted waves is $R_{+1} = A_{h}/A_{0} = \pm\sqrt{C_{-h}/C_{h}}$ . Yet the diffractive ratio is $R_{-1} = A_{h}/A_{0} = \pm\sqrt{C_{h}/C_{-h}}$ when the sign of the Bragg incident angle changes to positive, that is, $+\theta_{B}$ . Here, $C_{h}, C_{-h}$ are the Fourier coefficients of the modulated refractive index, whose Fourier expansion can be expressed as $n'(x) = C_{0} + C_{h}\exp(ihx) + C_{-h}\exp(-ihx)$ . The Fourier coefficients of the three media shown in Fig. 1(a) are written as

$$
\begin{array}{l l l} C _ {0} ^ {o} = 0, & C _ {h} ^ {o} = (n _ {r} + n _ {i}) / 2, & C _ {- h} ^ {o} = (n _ {r} - n _ {i}) / 2, \\ C _ {0} ^ {e} = \frac {1}{4} (n _ {r} - i n _ {i}), & C _ {h} ^ {e} = \frac {1}{2 \pi} (n _ {r} + n _ {i}), & C _ {- h} ^ {e} = \frac {1}{2 \pi} (n _ {r} - n _ {i}), \\ C _ {0} ^ {r} = \frac {1}{2} (n _ {r} - i n _ {i}), & C _ {h} ^ {r} = \frac {1}{\pi} (n _ {r} + n _ {i}), & C _ {- h} ^ {r} = \frac {1}{\pi} (n _ {r} - n _ {i}). \end{array}\tag{1}
$$

The superscripts o, e, and r represent the original exact PT-symmetric medium, the existing passive PT-symmetric medium, and the revised passive PT-symmetric medium, respectively. For all these PT-symmetric media, $C_{h}$ and $C_{-h}$ contain components of $n_{r} + n_{i}$ and $n_{r} - n_{i}$ , respectively. When the modulation amplitudes of the real and imaginary parts are equal, that is, $n_{r} = n_{i}$ , the diffraction order corresponding to $\exp(-ihx)$ will be suppressed. For the exact PT-symmetric medium and revised passive PT-symmetric medium, $R_{+1}$ will equal to zero at EP, which means the positive first-order diffraction with a negative incident angle will vanish completely. The considered diffraction beams in the proposed grating are the directly transmitted wave and the lowest-order diffracted wave. These beams are the only propagating modes in the AADG, while other higher-order diffractions are all evanescent. As a result, there is no disturbance of other diffraction orders in the designed AADG. However, there are redundant diffraction orders corresponding to $\exp(ihx/2)$ and $\exp(-ihx/2)$ for previous passive PT-symmetric media because of doubled periods (see details in Supplemental Material [41]). Comparing these Fourier coefficients, $C_{0}$ of passive PT-symmetric media cannot remain zero any longer due to the manual truncation of the refractive index. Usually, the average loss bias can be regarded as the loss of the background medium in passive PT-symmetric systems.

Diffraction in the proposed AADG with ideal parameters has been simulated with COMSOL Multiphysics. The refractive indices of three modulated parts are $n_{1}^{\prime}=0.16$ , $n_{2}^{\prime}=-0.16\delta i$ , and $n_{3}^{\prime}=0.16-0.16\delta i$ , respectively. Here, $\delta$ is the modulation ratio between the imaginary part and the real part. In the simulation, a pair of spatial Gaussian beams with Bragg incident angles are propagated through the passive PT-symmetric grating. The integral energy of separated diffractive beams in the far field is shown in Fig. 2. $I_{-1}(I_{+1})$ is the sound energy of the negative first-order (positive first-order) diffraction with a positive (negative) incident angle, which is normalized by the sound energy of the zero-order diffraction. In Fig. 2(a), the positive first-order diffraction is suppressed completely at EP, while the negative first-order diffraction remains at a high value with different modulation ratios. Because a unidirectional wave vector is generated in the diffraction grating when the modulation reaches the balanced condition $n_{r}=n_{i}$ , sound energy only couples to the negative first-order diffraction but cannot couple to the positive first-order diffraction. Figure 2(b) shows the intensity contrast between the negative first-order diffraction and the positive first-order diffraction with different modulation ratios, which reaches a prominent peak at EP.

## B. Realization and fabrication of modulators

In Fig. 3(a), the real part of the refractive index increases monotonically upon increasing the heights of additional cavities, while the imaginary part of the refractive index is not susceptible to the variation of the heights. As shown in Fig. 3(b), the adjustment of the radii of leaked holes can effectively modulate the imaginary part of the refractive index. These two unit cells almost modulate the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index independently, so we combine the additional cavities and leaked holes to modulate the real and imaginary parts simultaneously. The composite unit cell is shown in the inset of Fig. 3(c): additional cavities are still attached on the top plate of the waveguide, then leaked holes are opened on the ceiling of the additional cavities. The composite unit cell provides two adjustable geometric parameters to obtain the desired complex refractive index. In Fig. 3(c), the narrow colorful areas denote the target's real and imaginary parameters for the refractive index. The intersection of the two areas helps us to confirm the heights of additional cavities and radii of leaked holes. The final refractive indices of three manufactured modulators are $n_{1}^{\prime}=0.16$ , $n_{2}^{\prime}=0.03-0.16i$ , and $n_{3}^{\prime}=0.17-0.15i$ , respectively. The modulated refractive indices endure a little deviation by surrendering to the fabrication precision of sample pieces. In practice, three kinds of modulators are arranged side by side to form a sample piece as shown in Fig. 3(d). The width of each modulator is 3 cm equaling to 1/4 period, as the period is T=12 cm. Ten sample pieces are installed periodically on the top plate to form a diffraction grating. It is worth noting that sound-absorbing cotton is paved on the leaked holes to absorb sound energy as much as possible. Full sound absorption can be obtained with an impedance-matching boundary condition [42]. Here, the relative impedance of sound-absorbing cotton is $1.7+0.1i$ around 3.1 kHz, and the absorption coefficient is about 93%.

## C. Experimental demonstration of asymmetric diffraction

To experimentally verify the asymmetric diffraction effect of the proposed passive PT-symmetric grating, two rigid parallel acrylic plates (size: $1800 \times 3000 \times 10 \, mm^{3}$ ) are used to construct a two-dimensional (2D) waveguide with a spacing of 15 mm as shown in Fig. 3(d). There are ten periodical square openings on the top plate to install the sample pieces. Wedge absorbers made up of sound absorption cotton are mounted at the boundaries of the waveguide to minimize boundary reflections and isolate the inside sound field from outside noise. To generate the required incident spatial Gaussian beams, 24 loudspeakers (HiVi B1S) are used to assemble a liner array with an interval of 40 mm. All the speakers are synchronously driven by a 32-channel sound card (Antelope ORION 32HD) with different phases and amplitudes [41]. Two microphones (Brüel & Kjær type-4939 1/4 inch) are used to measure the sound pressure field inside the waveguide. One microphone is fixed as a reference throughout the entire mapping and the other is moved to extract local pressure at different positions in the x-z plane. The moving step length of the second microphone is 15 mm, whose movement is controlled by a motion stage.

Figure 4 presents the sound pressure fields at 3.1 kHz. First, a simulation under the same working conditions as the experimental configuration is implemented for comparison. As shown in Figs. 4(a) and 4(c), a pair of oblique incident spatial Gaussian beams is emitted from the top edge of the waveguide in the simulation. The positive first-order diffraction with a negative incident angle disappears, while the negative first-order diffraction with a positive incident angle is still observed clearly. The symmetrically distributed measured areas of $90 \times 36 \, cm^{2}$ are marked as I and II by white boxes. The measured pressure fields and the corresponding simulated ones with an enlarged view are shown in Figs. 4(b) and 4(d). The positive first-order diffraction (area I) is much weaker than the negative first-order diffraction (area II) in both simulated and experimental results. The results agree well with the theoretical model that unidirectional energy coupling at EP will cause asymmetric diffraction in a passive PT-symmetric grating.

Since the effective refractive indices of modulators remain steady in a wide frequency range [41], the asymmetric diffraction effect of the designed passive PT-symmetric grating is available in a broad frequency band. Measured sound pressure fields of three other frequencies are displayed in Fig. 5(a). In the normalized sound pressure fields, all the positive first-order diffractions with negative incident angles (left panel) are much weaker than negative first-order diffractions with positive incident angles (right panel). Figure 5(b) shows the simulated diffraction intensity contrast under the same conditions as the experimental configuration, where the sound energy of two diffracted waves differs by two orders of magnitude. Corresponding experimental results are displayed in Fig. 5(c). For mitigating the impact of weak reflection from the boundaries of the waveguide, the values of intensity bars $I_{-1}$ ( $I_{+1}$ ) are summations of acoustic energy in the measured areas, which are normalized by the energy summations of the negative first-order diffractions. The intensity bars $I_{+1}$ are all much lower than $I_{-1}$ in the measured frequency range, which demonstrates the broadband availability of the AADG base on the revised passive PT-symmetric medium.

## III. SUMMARY

In conclusion, we propose and experimentally realize an AADG based on a passive PT-symmetric medium. Because of the interferential diffraction beams caused by utilizing second-order Bragg scattering of the existing passive PT-symmetric medium, we change the period of the passive PT-symmetric medium back to that of the exact PT-symmetric medium. Unit cells combing additional cavities and leaked holes are introduced to simultaneously modulate the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index. The AADG based on the revised passive PT-symmetric medium retains no disturbance of other diffraction orders and has a stronger diffraction ability with more compact modulation. In both simulated and measured results, asymmetric diffraction of the designed acoustic grating is observed obviously at EP. The positive first-order diffractions with negative incident angles disappear, while there is no impact on the negative first-order diffractions with positive incident angles. Theoretically, the positive first-order diffraction should be suppressed completely at the exceptional point. There are some possible reasons for the weak signal in the measurement of the positive first-order diffraction, including the fabrication errors of samples and incomplete absorption at the boundaries of the waveguide.

Our study proposes an easily fabricated and tunable structure to construct the complex potential for a passive PT-symmetric medium. It broadens the way for designing functional PT-symmetric acoustic devices and will inspire further investigation of non-Hermitian acoustic systems. In addition, the designed AADG provides a feasible way to manipulate acoustic beams, which may have applications in noise control and beam forming.

## APPENDIX: COUPLED-MODE THEORY

The linear acoustic wave equation in the PT-symmetric grating can be written as

$$
\Delta P + k _ {0} ^ {2} n ^ {2} P = 0,\tag{A1}
$$

where $\Delta = \partial^{2}/\partial x^{2} + \partial^{2}/\partial z^{2}$ is the Laplacian, P is the sound pressure, and $k_{0} = \omega/c_{0}$ is the wave number of the background medium. The refractive index is given as $n(x) = n_{0} + n'(x)$ . In a weak coupling regime, the acoustic wave equation can be approximated to

$$
\Delta P + k _ {0} ^ {2} (n _ {0} ^ {2} + 2 n _ {0} n ^ {\prime}) P = 0.\tag{A2}
$$

Here, we focus on the first-order Bragg scattering of the PT-symmetric grating. The high-order diffractions can be negligible in the studied frequency range. The Fourier expansion of the modulated refractive index is $n'(x) = C_0 + C_h \exp(ihx) + C_{-h} \exp(-ihx)$ . For the incident monochromatic plane wave at Bragg angle $\theta_B[2k_0 \sin(\theta_B) = h]$ , as shown in Fig. 1(b) of the main text, the sound pressure in the grating contains two main coupled diffractive waves. A general expression is written as

$$
P (\mathbf {r}) = A _ {0} e ^ {- i \mathbf {q} _ {0} \mathbf {r}} + A _ {h} e ^ {- i \mathbf {q} _ {h} \mathbf {r}},\tag{A3}
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_{0}=(q_{0x},q_{oz}),\mathbf{q}_{h}=(q_{hx},q_{hz})$ are wave vectors of the zero-order and positive first-order (negative first-order) diffracted waves in the structure. When the sign of Bragg incident angle is negative, that is, $-\theta_{B}$ , the relationship between the components of wave vectors can be expressed as $q_{hx}=q_{0x}+h$ , $q_{hz}=q_{0z}$ . By substituting Eq. (A3) into Eq. (A2), we obtain the following coupled-mode equations

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} (- q _ {0 x} ^ {2} - q _ {0 z} ^ {2} + k _ {0} ^ {2} n _ {0} ^ {2} + 2 k _ {0} ^ {2} n _ {0} C _ {0}) A _ {0} + 2 k _ {0} ^ {2} n _ {0} C _ {h} A _ {h} = 0 \\ 2 k _ {0} ^ {2} n _ {0} C _ {- h} A _ {0} + (- q _ {h x} ^ {2} - q _ {h z} ^ {2} + k _ {0} ^ {2} n _ {0} ^ {2} + 2 k _ {0} ^ {2} n _ {0} C _ {0}) A _ {h} = 0 \end{array} \right.,\tag{A4}
$$

where $q_{0x} = \sin (\theta_B)k_0$ , which follows from Snell's law. The existence of nontrivial solutions of the system expressed by Eq. (A4) allows us to write down the dispersion relation for $z$ projections of wave vectors

$$
q _ {0 z} ^ {2} = k _ {0} ^ {2} n _ {0} ^ {2} + 2 k _ {0} ^ {2} n _ {0} C _ {0} - q _ {0 x} ^ {2} \pm 2 k _ {0} ^ {2} n _ {0} \sqrt {C _ {h} C _ {- h}}.\tag{A5}
$$

The two modes of Eq. (A5) represent the upper and lower deviations of the z directional wave vector due to the periodic modulation of the refractive index. Combining Eq. (A4) and Eq. (A5), the following relationship for the amplitudes of diffractive waves can be obtained

$$
R _ {+ 1} = \frac {A _ {h}}{A _ {0}} = \pm \sqrt {\frac {C _ {- h}}{C _ {h}}},\tag{A6}
$$

where $R_{+1}$ is the ratio between the amplitude coefficients of the positive first-order diffraction and the zero-order diffraction. On the other hand, when the sign of the Bragg incident angle changes to positive, that is, $+\theta_{B}$ , the relationship between the x directional projections of wave vectors in the PT-symmetric diffraction grating changes from $q_{hx} = q_{0x} + h$ to $q_{hx} = q_{0x} - h$ . As a result, the Fourier coefficients in Eq. (A4) change between $C_{h}$ and $C_{-h}$ . The corresponding diffraction intensity ratio naturally changes to $R_{-1}=A_{h}/A_{0}=\pm\sqrt{C_{h}/C_{-h}}$ .
